---
id: c-matrix-ops
title: Matrix Multiply and Transpose
difficulty: Medium
order: 1
tags: 2D arrays, flat arrays, cache order
---
## Statement
Read matrix A (`n × m`) and matrix B (`m × p`) with integer entries, and print:

1. the product C = A × B (`n × p`), using `long long` entries
2. the transpose of C (`p × n`)
3. the trace of C·Cᵀ (the sum of the squares of all C's entries), modulo 10^9 + 7

Store the matrices as **flat** `malloc`'d arrays indexed `i * cols + j`, and use the cache-friendly i-k-j loop order. Dimensions go up to 300.

## Starter
```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main(void) {
    int n, m, p;
    if (scanf("%d %d %d", &n, &m, &p) != 3) return 1;

    return 0;
}
```

## Hints
- `long long *C = calloc((size_t)n * p, sizeof *C);` starts zeroed.
- i-k-j order: `for i, for k: aik = A[i*m + k]; for j: C[i*p + j] += aik * B[k*p + j];`.
- The sum of squares: reduce `(c % MOD) * (c % MOD)`, handling negative `c`.

## Solution
```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

#define MOD 1000000007LL

int main(void) {
    int n, m, p;
    if (scanf("%d %d %d", &n, &m, &p) != 3) return 1;
    long long *A = malloc(sizeof *A * (size_t)n * m);
    long long *B = malloc(sizeof *B * (size_t)m * p);
    long long *C = calloc((size_t)n * p, sizeof *C);
    if (!A || !B || !C) return 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < n * m; i++) scanf("%lld", &A[i]);
    for (int i = 0; i < m * p; i++) scanf("%lld", &B[i]);

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        for (int k = 0; k < m; k++) {
            long long aik = A[i * m + k];
            for (int j = 0; j < p; j++)
                C[i * p + j] += aik * B[k * p + j];
        }

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j < p; j++)
            printf("%lld%c", C[i * p + j], j == p - 1 ? '\n' : ' ');
    for (int j = 0; j < p; j++)
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            printf("%lld%c", C[i * p + j], i == n - 1 ? '\n' : ' ');

    long long tr = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n * p; i++) {
        long long c = ((C[i] % MOD) + MOD) % MOD;
        tr = (tr + c * c) % MOD;
    }
    printf("%lld\n", tr);
    free(A); free(B); free(C);
    return 0;
}
```

In i-k-j order the innermost loop walks `B` and `C` **row-wise** (consecutive addresses). The textbook i-j-k order walks `B` down a column, a cache miss on every step. For 300×300 the difference is small. At 2000×2000 it's several times. This is the first optimisation step behind BLAS libraries like OpenBLAS, which NumPy calls for `@`.
